subtype: Ducking and defensive reflex in danger [Regulating]
passage: Note from Mr. Mridul, campus safety volunteer. On Friday evening I was at the crossing outside the gate when two motorbike riders began shouting at each other over a near-miss. A crowd gathered. Sumit, a first-year student who had stopped to wait for the light, dropped low, covered the back of the head with one arm and stepped back behind a parked auto. I saw the crouch as a quick protective move, not fear alone. When one rider grabbed the other's collar, Sumit walked off and phoned the guard post. Afterwards I told Sumit that leaving early was the sensible choice, and I asked whether a short safety session for first-years would help. Sumit said it would.

qa.q: Where did Mridul see the argument?
qa.a: Mridul saw it at the crossing outside the gate.

qa.q: What was Sumit likely feeling when dropping low and stepping back?
qa.a: Sumit was probably alarmed and wanted to get out of harm's way; the quick crouch and retreat show self-protection. It may have been a reflex more than a decision, so it is not proof of panic.

qa.q: What did Sumit do that worked better than staying to watch?
qa.a: Sumit moved away early and phoned the guard post, rather than trying to intervene or prove anything.

qa.q: How might the riders have seen the crowd around them?
qa.a: The crowd could have made the argument worse or kept it going, which is why getting help and leaving is safer than joining in.

grounding: A young adult drops low, covers the head and moves away from a fight risk, and leaving early and getting help works better than bravado.

subtype: Ducking and defensive reflex in danger [Regulating]
passage: Diary, 11 pm. Joseph writing. Outside the tea stall today Reena and I saw two guys arguing over a parked scooter. It got loud fast. One of them kept shouting, "Say it again!" and the other stepped right up to his face. My body did something before my brain did: my shoulders dropped, my hands came up near my head and I took a step back. Reena tugged my sleeve and said, "Let's go." We crossed to the other side, and Reena texted the shop owner that there was a fight starting. I felt shaky after, and a bit silly, but I'm glad we didn't stay. Walking away wasn't losing.

qa.q: What were the two men arguing over?
qa.a: The two men were arguing over a parked scooter.
Joseph felt shaky and a little silly, though glad to have left. The shakiness suggests the body still reacted to the danger even after they were safe.

qa.q: What steps did Joseph and Reena take that helped?
qa.a: They crossed to the other side of the road and Reena texted the shop owner about the fight, instead of watching or trying to stop it.

qa.q: How might the shop owner have seen Reena's text?
qa.a: The shop owner probably saw it as a helpful warning so they could keep customers safe or call for help.

grounding: A young adult ducks and steps away when a fight risk appears, and leaving early and getting help protects better than bravado.
